summary:
Space Mission Hub is an interactive aerospace engineering and rocket design simulation platform developed in Godot 4.3 with Google Gemini AI integration.

The project tackles the barrier to entry in space exploration education by turning complex textbook systems engineering into an engaging, hands-on, gamified experience.

The platform features two complementary modes:

Space Mission Game: A collaborative systems engineering simulator (solo or up to 4 local players) where participants take on authentic roles (Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, Telemetry Engineer). Teams design missions (Climate Watch, Space Weather, Lunar Mapper, Telecom Relay) while balancing real-world trade-offs: payload mass, orbital eclipse power deficits, solar array degradation, telemetry link budgets, radiation hardening, and launch costs.

Rocket Constructor: A CAD rocketry module with atmospheric flight physics (aerodynamic drag, max-Q dynamic pressure limits, Tsiolkovsky propellant consumption, landing) and AI engineering verification via Gemini 2.5 Flash.

Utilizing 100% procedurally synthesized 3D models, planet textures, and audio, it runs anywhere without external asset bloat.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Space Mission Hub is an interactive aerospace educational simulation platform built on Godot 4.3 that seamlessly integrates two complementary modes:
Space Mission Game (space_mission_game):
Players (solo or a hotseat team of up to 4 players on one computer) take on specialized engineering roles: Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Telemetry Engineer. They select one of four real-world objectives:
Climate Watch: Earth climate, temperature, and vegetation monitoring.
Space Weather Sentinel: tracking solar flares and Van Allen radiation belts.
Lunar Mapper: lunar topography and mineral spectroscopy.
Connect the Globe: geostationary telecommunications relay.
The team selects the orbit (LEO, SSO, MEO, GEO, LLO), launch vehicle, bus structure, solar array size, battery capacity, flight computer, attitude control system (ADCS), propellant mass, and scientific instruments. The simulator calculates in real time whether power will suffice during orbital eclipses, whether telemetry bandwidth (S, X, Ka bands) can handle daily sensor generation, and whether storage buffers will overflow. Once launched, a step-by-step monthly simulation models orbital operations, cumulative science return, and random anomalies (solar flares, micrometeorite strikes, single-event upsets), displayed on synchronized 2D orbital tracks and 3D views.
Rocket Constructor (rocket_constructor):
A dedicated modular CAD module where users configure launch vehicle stages (engines, propellant tanks, fairings, stabilization fins). Custom designs are dispatched to a local Python AI server where Google Gemini 2.5 Flash, backed by live web search via DuckDuckGo, checks physical plausibility (realistic thrust-to-weight ratios and structural limits) and provides constructive engineering feedback. Approved rockets launch in a numerical flight simulator with authentic physics: thrust, aerodynamic atmospheric drag, dynamic pressure (max-Q), propellant depletion, and powered vertical landing recovery.
What benefits does your project have?
Authentic Systems Engineering Mindset: Unlike arcade games focused solely on steering, Space Mission Hub teaches that no aerospace decision exists in a vacuum. Choosing a heavier radar demands larger solar arrays and batteries, increasing spacecraft mass and requiring a significantly more expensive launch vehicle.
Team Collaboration: The hotseat multi-role mode requires team members to negotiate trade-offs between scientific ambitions, power budgets, and financial constraints before signing off on the mission.
Intelligent AI Mentorship: Gemini AI serves as a virtual Chief Engineer. It does not just accept or reject; it provides constructive feedback comparing designs to real aerospace engines.
Universal Accessibility: With 100% procedurally generated meshes, planet textures, and audio waveforms, the application is tiny in size, requires no large asset downloads, and runs smoothly on standard school computers without requiring an internet connection.
What is the expected impact?
Demystifying Aerospace Education: Enables students and space enthusiasts to gain hands-on experience in mission architecture and rocketry.
Ready-to-Use STEM Classroom Tool: Fully open-source with low hardware requirements and an offline rule-based fallback mode, making it immediately viable for high school physics classes, coding workshops, and university engineering clubs.
What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
Game Engine: Godot Engine 4.3 (GDScript language, GL Compatibility renderer for broad hardware compatibility).
AI Backend: Python 3.10+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic.
AI Model: Google GenAI SDK (Gemini 2.5 Flash).
Live Grounding: DuckDuckGo Search API (ddgs package) for verifying real-world rocket engine parameters.
Procedural Audio: Godot AudioStreamGenerator (mathematical PCM 16-bit synthesis of button clicks, thrusters, and telemetry tones).
Visuals: Godot procedural primitives and noise texture generators for dynamic 3D spacecraft and Earth/Moon rendering.
How creative is your project?
Complete Zero-Asset Procedural Architecture: The project bundles zero external 3D models or audio clips. Spacecraft geometry, planetary atmospheric shaders, and acoustic sound waves are computed algorithmically at runtime.
Grounded AI Design Review Board: Rather than using an LLM as a generic text chatbot, Gemini is integrated directly into the engineering workflow, evaluating student parameters against live web benchmarks.
What factors did your team consider?
Orbital Mechanics and Sunlight Geometry:
Solar illumination and eclipse durations across orbits (on LEO the craft spends 40% of each 90-minute orbit in Earth's shadow, while Sun-Synchronous Orbit offers nearly continuous sunlight).
Ground station line-of-sight pass windows: low orbits only provide short contact windows per pass, whereas geostationary orbits offer permanent direct visibility.
Power Budgets and Environmental Degradation:
Solar cell degradation from cosmic radiation over time (2% to 5% efficiency loss per year depending on the orbital altitude).
Battery capacity sizing ensuring power continuity through eclipse periods to avoid fatal brownouts.
Telemetry Link Budgets and Data Management:
Data generation rates versus downlink channel capacity (S-band: 80 GB/day, X-band: 300 GB/day, Ka-band: 900 GB/day).
Solid-state buffer saturation: excess data that cannot be downlinked during station passes overflows and is lost.
Flight Dynamics and Atmospheric Aerodynamics:
Exponential barometric atmospheric density model decaying with altitude.
Dynamic pressure (max-Q): aerodynamic stress depends on air density and velocity squared. Exceeding structural pressure limits breaks the rocket if throttle is not reduced through the thick lower atmosphere.
Tsiolkovsky propellant mass flow: propellant consumption calculated from specific impulse (280 seconds) and engine thrust.
Touchdown criteria: retro-propulsion throttle control to ensure landing velocity remains under 12 meters per second.
Radiation Hardening and Spacecraft Reliability:
Radiation-hardened flight computers and composite structural shielding to safeguard against Single Event Upsets (SEUs) from cosmic rays and solar flares.
Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS) pointing accuracy directly impacting scientific observation resolution.
